name: Murray Aitkin
affiliation: University of Newcastle / University of Western Australia
key_contribution: Applied Simpson's Paradox to posterior Bayes factors; his work prompted Lindley's counter-example and is the proximate occasion for the Bayesian tradition's engagement with the paradox.
signature_work: Aitkin (1991/1997) — posterior Bayes factor papers, JRSS-B
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Part of an internal Bayesian dispute; the paradox appears as a consistency problem in model selection, not as an aggregation or confounding problem in Pearl's sense

name: Abolfazl Asudeh
key_contribution: Teaches and researches Simpson's Paradox as a core topic in responsible data science and AI fairness; frames it as a foundational structural threat to fairness audits in heterogeneous datasets.
signature_work: CS516 course materials and related research at UIC (2025)
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Bridges the Hannan aggregation-bias framing and the AI fairness audit literature; treats the paradox as a data-engineering problem, not purely a causal inference problem

name: C. R. Blyth
key_contribution: Coined the term "Simpson's Paradox" (1972), provided the first formal definition, and framed the reversal as a genuine logical paradox rather than a statistical curiosity.
signature_work: Blyth (1972) — On Simpson's Paradox and the Sure-Thing Principle, JASA
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Blyth's formal definition is one of three non-equivalent definitions in the literature (Blyth 1972, Mittal 1991, Bandyopadhyay et al. 2011); Pearl's framework dissolves the definitional ambiguity via causal structure

name: Nancy Cartwright
key_contribution: Proposed the influential resolution (1979): a cause must raise the probability of its effect in every homogeneous background context, not just in the aggregate. Argued purely statistical accounts of causation fail.
signature_work: Cartwright (1979) — Causal Laws and Effective Strategies, Nous
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Cartwright's "background contexts" anticipate stratification in Pearl's sense; Pearl acknowledges Cartwright but argues DAGs make the notion precise and computable

name: Alexandra Chouldechova
key_contribution: Proved the fairness impossibility theorem (2017): when recidivism prevalence differs across groups, satisfying calibration necessarily produces disparate error rates — base-rate divergence (the paradox mechanism) makes irreconcilable fairness criteria structurally unavoidable.
signature_work: Chouldechova (2017) — Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact, Big Data journal (arXiv:1610.07524)
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Translates the paradox into ML fairness: the "confounder" is group membership; the "strata" are demographic subgroups; the reversal is which group appears disadvantaged depending on the metric chosen. Not framed in Pearl's DAG language but structurally equivalent.

name: Cohen & Nagel
key_contribution: First documented sign reversal specifically (association flipping direction, not merely disappearing), predating Simpson's 1951 paper.
signature_work: Cohen & Nagel (1934) — An Introduction to Logic and Scientific Method
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Provided the logical/philosophical framing that the philosophy-of-science tradition (Cartwright, Eells) built on

name: Dong, Cai & Zhao
key_contribution: Challenged Pearl's confounding-centric account (2024): identified three classes of Simpson's Paradox that occur without confounding — inter-unit causation, accidental associations, and inappropriate aggregate variables.
signature_work: Dong, Cai & Zhao (2024) — European Journal for Philosophy of Science
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Direct critique of Pearl: argues the DAG back-door criterion is insufficient as a universal resolution because not all reversals are confounding artifacts

name: Ellery Eells
key_contribution: Defended Cartwright's resolution against Richard Otte's (1985) critique; published Probabilistic Causality (1991), the most systematic treatment of the probabilistic causality tradition.
signature_work: Eells (1991) — Probabilistic Causality, Cambridge University Press
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Eells's defence of Cartwright against Otte closes off one branch of the philosophy debate; Pearl's DAG approach is seen by many as the operationalisation that finally settled it

name: Sander Greenland
key_contribution: Linked Simpson's Paradox to noncollapsibility (2021): the failure of a group-level measure to equal a simple average of subgroup measures. Distinguishes noncollapsibility from confounding — the two are commonly conflated.
signature_work: Greenland (2021) — Noncollapsibility, confounding, and sparse-data bias, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Collaborated with Pearl (Greenland, Robins & Pearl 1999, Statistical Science) on confounding and collapsibility. Greenland operationalises the paradox for epidemiological practice where Pearl's do-calculus is abstract.

name: Dennis Lindley
key_contribution: Showed (1997) that Bayes factor proponents can simultaneously conclude tall men > tall women, short men > short women, yet women > men overall — a Simpson reversal inside Bayesian hypothesis testing. Lindley himself noted the connection.
signature_work: Lindley (1997) — counter-example to Aitkin's posterior Bayes factor, JRSS-B
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Orthogonal to both Hannan and Pearl: Lindley shows the paradox is not merely a frequentist aggregation problem but appears inside the Bayesian framework's own model-selection machinery

name: Karl Pearson
key_contribution: First (1899) observed that marginal and partial associations between continuous variables can differ, producing spurious correlations — the pre-Simpson precursor.
signature_work: Pearson et al. (1899) — early work on genetic inheritance and spurious correlation
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Predates both; Pearl's DAG tradition explicitly cites Pearson as the origin point of the confusion his framework resolves

name: Hans Reichenbach
key_contribution: Developed the Common Cause Principle (1956): every statistical correlation has a causal explanation, either direct causation or a common cause. This principle frames the paradox as a symptom of an uncontrolled common cause.
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Pearl's backdoor criterion is a formalisation of Reichenbach's common-cause screening-off idea in DAG language

name: James M. Robins
key_contribution: Developed marginal structural models and g-computation — causal inference methods for observational epidemiology that account for time-varying confounding, of which Simpson's Paradox is the canonical simple case.
signature_work: Greenland, Robins & Pearl (1999) — Confounding and Collapsibility in Causal Inference, Statistical Science
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Robins's g-methods and Pearl's do-calculus were developed independently and are now understood to be equivalent under certain conditions; both address the same confounding problem the paradox exposes

name: Edward H. Simpson
key_contribution: Gave the paradox its name by formalising sign reversal in contingency tables (1951 JRSS-B paper), though unaware of Cohen & Nagel's earlier sign-reversal documentation.
signature_work: Simpson (1951) — The Interpretation of Interaction in Contingency Tables, JRSS-B
relation_to_hannan_pearl: The naming origin; Pearl's r414.pdf distinguishes Simpson's formal contribution from the deeper causal question Simpson himself did not answer

name: Spirtes, Glymour & Scheines
key_contribution: The CMU group (SGS) developed constraint-based causal discovery (PC/FCI algorithms) as a parallel DAG tradition to Pearl's. Their 2000 book explicitly names clarifying Simpson's Paradox as a goal.
signature_work: Spirtes, Glymour & Scheines (2000) — Causation, Prediction, and Search, MIT Press
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Methodologically distinct from Pearl: SGS uses constraint-based structure discovery from conditional independence tests; Pearl uses do-calculus and interventional logic. Both treat the paradox as a confounding problem but differ in how to identify confounders from data.

name: Patrick Suppes
key_contribution: Developed probabilistic causality theory (1970): causes raise the probability of their effects. The paradox shows this is necessary but insufficient — background context must be held fixed.
signature_work: Suppes (1970) — A Probabilistic Theory of Causality
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Suppes's framework is the direct predecessor Cartwright critiques and extends; Pearl's do-calculus supersedes probabilistic causality by making interventions explicit

name: Sharma, Kaushik, Peious & Draheim
affiliation: Tallinn University of Technology — Information Systems Group
key_contribution: Extended Simpson's Paradox detection from categorical to continuous variables for ML fairness audits (2022); frames automated paradox detection as a step toward next-generation fairness platforms.
signature_work: Sharma et al. (2022) — Detecting Simpson's Paradox: A Step Towards Fairness in Machine Learning, Springer
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Extends Hannan-style aggregation detection into continuous feature spaces; does not use Pearl's causal framework but treats the paradox as a data-pattern detection problem

name: G. Udny Yule
key_contribution: Extended Pearson's observation (1903) to categorical data; the phenomenon is sometimes called the Yule–Simpson effect.
signature_work: Yule (1903) — Notes on the theory of association of attributes in statistics
relation_to_hannan_pearl: Provides the categorical-data framing that Hannan's aggregation bias literature builds on; Pearl's back-door criterion addresses exactly what Yule's correlations could not distinguish
